newsitem.title: USA: US budget deal? Yes. Wall St rally? No. -- experts.
newsitem.headline: US budget deal? Yes. Wall St rally? No. -- experts.

text.p: Wall Street appears confident the Clinton Administration and the Republican-led Congress will clinch a balanced budget deal in 1997, U.S. experts said.
But they warned: Don't expect a major drop in long-term interest rates and a massive equity buying spree in hope of an agreement.
Democrats and Republicans have been holding talks on balancing the budget for well over a year.

But the subject gained momentum recently as the White House and Republican leaders appear to have adopted a more conciliatory tone just days before President Bill Clinton unveils his fiscal 1998 budget plan on February 6.

Most economists seem to have a balanced budget agreement factored into their forecasts for 1997, including some Wall Street heavyweights. Goldman, Sachs and Co Inc, for example, sees an 80 percent chance a deal will be reached this year.
But Wall Street thinks a deal alone is not enough.

Pundits said the market wants to be convinced the agreed program will go beyond political rhetoric and tackle one of the most important problems haunting U.S. public finances -- the revamping of entitlement programs.
"The entitlements are the key issue," said Richard Berner, chief economist at Mellon Bank Corp.

Analysts said an overhaul of programs such as Social Security, Medicare and Medicaid is a must to keep federal finances sound early into the next century, when the first batch of baby boomers will be eligible for retirement.
This issue is perceived by many as one of the main hurdles to be surpassed during budget negotiations.
Clinton's proposals to revamp Medicare include $138 billion in cuts over six years, relying mostly on cuts in payments to health care providers.
Some Republicans, including Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, have already voiced opposition to Clinton's plan, saying the cuts were not enough to rescue the endangered program.
Medicare's hospital trust fund is estimated to go bankrupt in 2001 without program changes.

With little left to be cut from discretionary spending and the military budget, analysts said Wall Street is also paying special attention to what the two sides are planning to do with the other side of the equation -- revenues.
Oddly enough, instead of higher taxes, Republicans and Democrats alike are working on tax relief programs, much more likely to be implemented sooner rather than later.
Clinton's plan involves tax credits and deductions, while the Republican proposal calls for lower tax rates and smaller government. The two sides seem to agree that tax cuts should be front-loaded.

"What is going to be a little bit disappointing is that I think the fiscal restraint will be back-loaded going into the years 2000, 2001 and 2002," said William Dudley, chief economist at Goldman, Sachs.

"So fiscal policy in 1997 and 1998 will probably be broadly neutral. So the Federal Reserve is not going to be able to look at a balanced budget agreement and say, 'Oh, we can ease monetary policy,'" the chief economist said.

On top of that, analysts said expectations for stronger economic growth in 1997 combined with fears of higher labor costs and increasing inflation pressures are expected keep interest rates high regardless of the budget scenario.

"We'll see growth exceeding expectations and an upward trajectory in wage and inflationary pressures. Those will be the primary influences on how Treasuries move in 1997," said Kevin Flanagan, vice president at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.
"A balanced budget agreement could alleviate the rise in rates, but it won't prevent it," he added.
William Griggs, a former deputy assistant secretary for economic policy at the U.S. Treasury, agreed.
"My thought is that a budget agreement doesn't guarantee you don't have inflation," said Griggs, who is currently the managing director at consulting firm Griggs and Santow Inc.
"Nor does it mean you'll avoid recessions, nor does it mean you'll avoid booms. It really doesn't guarantee you anything," Griggs added.
The benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond yield is quoted around 6.84 percent and most analysts believe that rate will likely reach 7.25 percent before it crawls back to 6.50 percent.
"That is regardless of what might happen to the budget talks in Washington," said the head of the Treasury desk at a major U.S. investment bank, who asked not to be named.
"The budget deal as it has been presented will be very important to the market in the long term. But in our everyday trading lives, the economic scene is likely to prevail," the head trader added.
